name: Microsound
editorial_article: Microsound is an avant-garde genre of experimental electronic music characterized by its focus on sound at extremely granular time scales, often lasting mere milliseconds. Arising in the late 1990s and flourishing in the early 2000s, it functions as a digital-era evolution of musique concrète, utilizing advanced signal processing techniques like granular synthesis and micromontage to manipulate audio at a sub-note level. By prioritizing the arrangement of tiny sound particles—clicks, pulses, glitches, and static textures—artists in this field essentially treat audio as a tangible, physical substance, stripping away traditional melodic or harmonic expectations to explore the architecture of sound itself. \n\nOften described as a cousin to the glitch genre, microsound distinguishes itself through its often starker, more analytical aesthetic, favoring precision and timbral exploration. The movement is deeply tied to digital aesthetics, where the constraints and possibilities of computer-based synthesis enabled the fine-grained control necessary to sculpt these micro-events. Key figures like Alva Noto, Ryoji Ikeda, and Fennesz have been instrumental in defining this sound, often bridging the gap between minimalist electronic music and ambient soundscapes. The genre demands an active, microscopic mode of listening, inviting the audience to engage with the subtle shifts, density, and spatialization of sound within the digital void, ultimately creating an immersive experience that redefines the relationship between digital technology and musical structure.
editorial_definition: Microsound is an experimental electronic music genre that explores the aesthetic possibilities of audio manipulated at extremely short time scales, often using granular synthesis and digital signal processing to construct compositions from micro-events.
